newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Gulf Arabs fret over U.S. approach on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs fret over U.S. approach on Iraq.

text.p: Some of America's Gulf Arab allies say privately they are irritated by what they see as a go-it-alone U.S. policy over Iraq that has ignored their concern about Washington's high-stakes confrontation with Baghdad.

"We read about it in the news...What kind of a partnership is this?" asked a senior Gulf Arab military official. "Even if (some) members of the coalition oppose this move or that policy, they (U.S.) still have to consult with us first."
That irritation is apparently not felt in Kuwait, which remains deeply grateful for American leadership of the 1991 Gulf War coalition that ended Iraq's seven-month occupation.

But any doubt that there was a need to improve wider Arab sentiment about American policy was dispelled on Tuesday when Kuwait began a diplomatic offensive to rebuild the post-war consensus on the need to contain Baghdad.
"Partnership means negotiations and consultations, not being surprised, out of the blue," added the official.

Gulf Arab officials say the first stirrings of concern were felt on September 3 and 4 when the U.S. fired 44 cruise missiles on Iraqi targets in southern Iraq, moves taken with the knowledge of some regional allies but without their approval.
Disapproval grew when Washington later began a big military buildup in the strategic region amid U.S. hints that possible fresh strikes against Baghdad were in the pipeline.
Concern deepened on Friday when many Gulf officials, apparently including Kuwaitis, learned of Washington's intention to send troops to Kuwait only from media reports from the U.S.
"If you think the Kuwaitis were upset, I tell you the Saudis were also offended," said another Gulf official about the dominant and strongest member of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Kuwait and Saudi Arabia are GCC members along with Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Qatar. They all have close military links with Washington.
Sources say Riyadh feels that it has the right to know of all military moves in the region ahead of time even if the deployment is not on its territory.
Saudi silence over the U.S. actions is widely seen as disapproval of American insensitivity towards the the political impact of such strikes on Gulf Arab opinion.

They said Washington's attacks on fellow Arab Iraq have exposed Gulf states to the accusation that they are lackeys of an alien superpower that is inimical to the conservative values and traditions of the region.

Saudi Arabia and non-Arab Turkey, Iraq's southern and northern neighbours respectively, have said that if asked they would have turned down a U.S. request to use their bases for attacks against Iraq in the current crisis. Both have Western aircraft enforcing no-fly zones over Iraq.
U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry met King Fahd of Saudi Arabia to try to resolve differences and explain what further possible military measures could be taken against Iraq.
He did the same in Bahrain, Turkey and Kuwait, which on Monday approved the deployment of U.S. forces.
Kuwait is now the only Arab state clearly in support of the U.S. military moves while its Arab allies appear opposed to wider strikes against Iraq.
American and Kuwait officials have in recent days repeatedly said that the Gulf War alliance was firmly in place.
Western analysts in Kuwait said they believed any fresh attack on Iraq would not disintegrate the coalition provided these were limited to air defences in the no-fly zones.

The senior Gulf Arab military official said: "A wider attack will ruin everything and could split the coalition...If they strike targets up to the 33rd parallel, some in the Gulf would be opposed, but would reluctantly stay silent."
Some analysts said current differences were less threatening to the alliance than when Iraq gained open support from some Gulf Arab states last year for the lifting of U.N. sanctions.
"That was a difficult period and they have passed through it. The alliance has not approached that level yet," one said.
